[{"order":1,"type":"heading","text":"Understanding MySQL Undo Logs and Purge Threads"},{"order":2,"type":"paragraph","text":"In MySQL InnoDB storage engine, maintaining ACID compliance, particularly atomicity and isolation, requires the use of undo logs. Undo logs are essentially a collection of rollback segments used to store the old versions of data modified by transactions."},{"order":3,"type":"subheading","text":"What is an Undo Log?"},{"order":4,"type":"paragraph","text":"When a transaction modifies data, InnoDB writes the previous state of the data into undo logs before applying the modifications. These logs serve two primary purposes:"},{"order":5,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Rollback Operations: If a transaction fails or explicitly executes a ROLLBACK statement, InnoDB uses the undo logs to revert the changes and restore the original data."},{"order":6,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Multi-Version Concurrency Control (MVCC): Concurrent readers can access older, consistent snapshots of data from the undo logs while another transaction is actively modifying the same rows."},{"order":7,"type":"subheading","text":"The Role of Purge Threads"},{"order":8,"type":"paragraph","text":"Over time, as transactions commit, the undo logs associated with those completed transactions are no longer needed for rollbacks or active MVCC reads. However, they cannot be immediately deleted because older snapshots might still be required by long-running transactions. The background processes responsible for cleaning up these obsolete undo logs are known as purge threads."},{"order":9,"type":"paragraph","text":"Purge threads continuously scan the undo logs, evaluate the read views of all active transactions, and safely remove (purge) undo log records that are no longer referenced. This reclamation process prevents undo logs from growing indefinitely and freeing up disk space."},{"order":10,"type":"subheading","text":"Configuring Undo Logs and Purge Threads"},{"order":11,"type":"paragraph","text":"MySQL provides several configuration variables to tune the performance of undo logs and purge threads, especially for heavily concurrent workloads. You can inspect the current configuration using SQL queries."},{"order":12,"type":"code","text":"SHOW VARIABLES LIKE 'innodb_purge_threads';
SHOW VARIABLES LIKE 'innodb_undo_logs';"},{"order":13,"type":"paragraph","text":"The innodb_purge_threads variable defines the number of background threads dedicated to the purge operation. Increasing this value can help systems with high write concurrency keep up with the generation of undo logs."},{"order":14,"type":"code","text":"[mysqld]
innodb_purge_threads = 4
innodb_undo_logs = 128"},{"order":15,"type":"subheading","text":"Monitoring Undo Log Health"},{"order":16,"type":"paragraph","text":"If purge threads fall behind the rate at which transactions generate undo logs, the undo tablespaces will grow rapidly. This condition is often referred to as undo log bloat. You can monitor the state of InnoDB engines using the INFORMATION_SCHEMA or Performance Schema."},{"order":17,"type":"code","text":"SELECT * FROM INFORMATION_SCHEMA.INNODB_TRX;"},{"order":18,"type":"paragraph","text":"A common cause for purge lag is a single long-running transaction that maintains an old read view, preventing purge threads from cleaning up any subsequent undo logs. Identifying and terminating such transactions is critical for maintaining database performance and preventing disk exhaustion."}]
